stories.headline: Reliance’s FMCG war chest swells
stories.title: Reliance’s FMCG war chest swells
stories.summary: Kolkata: Reliance Industries has quadrupled the authorised share capital of its rapidly expanding fast-moving consumer goods (FMCG) arm, Reliance Consumer Products (RCPL), to ₹40,000 crore, potentially giving it greater headroom for capital infusion, as well as increased its borrowing and investment limits, as it scales up the business, according to the latest regulatory filings with the Registrar of Companies.RCPL, which sells Campa Cola and the Independence range of staples, said the authorised share capital increase would facilitate the issuance of capital in view of the expanding scale of its FMCG operations.Also Read: Reliance Industries' FMCG business turns EBITDA positive for the first timeIt has also tripled its borrowing limit to ₹27,000 crore from ₹9,000 crore to meet the "increased fund requirement for the business". The limit for making investments in, or providing loans to, other companies has been doubled to ₹4,000 crore, according to the filings accessed through business intelligence platform Tofler.Reliance Industries has also extended the tenure of three executive directors-T Krishnakumar (66), Ketan Mody (49) and Asim Parekh (61)-by five years to 2030. The RCPL board approved the resolutions in July and August, the filings showed. Queries emailed to Reliance Industries remained unanswered until press time.RCPL had last December raised its authorised share capital to ₹10,000 crore as part of a restructuring of the parent group's FMCG business, following which the FMCG business became a direct subsidiary of Reliance Industries instead of being a subsidiary of Reliance Retail Ventures (RRVL).The restructuring involved the transfer of FMCG brands from Reliance Retail to RRVL through a slump sale.Also Read: Ambani uses ₹10 power again for the next disruption in a hot Indian marketThe then RCPL was then amalgamated with RRVL, following which the consolidated "consumer brands business undertaking" was demerged from RRVL into a new entity, Tira Beauty Ltd, which was subsequently rebranded as RCPL again.In its latest filings, RCPL said its "business outlook for FY 2026-27 and coming years is positive with both value and volume expected to grow".RCPL reported total income of ₹7,042 crore and a net loss of ₹125 crore for the period December 2025 to March 2026, according to the filings.

opening: Kolkata: Reliance Industries has quadrupled the authorised share capital of its rapidly expanding fast-moving consumer goods (FMCG) arm, Reliance Consumer Products (RCPL), to ₹40,000 crore, potentially giving it greater headroom for capital infusion, as well as increased its borrowing and investment limits, as it scales up the business, according to the latest regulatory filings with the Registrar of Companies.

RCPL, which sells Campa Cola and the Independence range of staples, said the authorised share capital increase would facilitate the issuance of capital in view of the expanding scale of its FMCG operations.
body: It has also tripled its borrowing limit to ₹27,000 crore from ₹9,000 crore to meet the "increased fund requirement for the business".
The limit for making investments in, or providing loans to, other companies has been doubled to ₹4,000 crore, according to the filings accessed through business intelligence platform Tofler.
Reliance Industries has also extended the tenure of three executive directors-T Krishnakumar (66), Ketan Mody (49) and Asim Parekh (61)-by five years to 2030.
The RCPL board approved the resolutions in July and August, the filings showed.
Queries emailed to Reliance Industries remained unanswered until press time.

RCPL had last December raised its authorised share capital to ₹10,000 crore as part of a restructuring of the parent group's FMCG business, following which the FMCG business became a direct subsidiary of Reliance Industries instead of being a subsidiary of Reliance Retail Ventures (RRVL).
The restructuring involved the transfer of FMCG brands from Reliance Retail to RRVL through a slump sale.

The then RCPL was then amalgamated with RRVL, following which the consolidated "consumer brands business undertaking" was demerged from RRVL into a new entity, Tira Beauty Ltd, which was subsequently rebranded as RCPL again.
RCPL reported total income of ₹7,042 crore and a net loss of ₹125 crore for the period December 2025 to March 2026, according to the filings.

bullets.text: In its latest filings, RCPL said its "business outlook for FY 2026-27 and coming years is positive with both value and volume expected to grow".

Reliance Industries has also extended the tenure of three executive directors-T Krishnakumar (66), Ketan Mody (49) and Asim Parekh (61)-by five years to 2030.
In its latest filings, RCPL said its "business outlook for FY 2026-27 and coming years is positive with both value and volume expected to grow".

stories.headline: Rana sets deadline for water, flood works
stories.title: Rana sets deadline for water, flood works
stories.summary: Srinagar, Sep 23: Minister for Jal Shakti, Forest, Ecology & Environment and Tribal Affairs, Javed Ahmed Rana, on Wednesday chaired a review meeting to assess the physical and financial progress of various schemes and developmental works being executed by the Jal Shakti Department and Irrigation & Flood Control (I&FC) Departments in Kashmir Division. The meeting was attended by Chief Engineers of the Jal Shakti and Irrigation & Flood Control Departments, besides all Superintending Engineers of the Hydraulic Circles of Kashmir Division. During the meeting, the concerned officers briefed the Minister on the progress of ongoing schemes, achievements recorded so far, bottlenecks and the status of expenditure against funds sanctioned and earmarked for different works. While reviewing the progress, the Minister directed the officers to accelerate execution of works on the ground and ensure that all projects nearing completion are completed within the prescribed timelines, particularly before the onset of winter. Reviewing the functioning and progress of the Jal Shakti Department, Rana directed the officers to accord top priority to all incomplete drinking water supply schemes and make every effort to commission them before the winter season sets in. He stressed the need for advanced functional testing of pipelines, pumping arrangements, storage tanks and other associated infrastructure so that any technical deficiencies are identified and rectified well in time. The Minister also called for close field-level monitoring of schemes and directed the concerned officers to undertake regular inspections of works, particularly those at advanced stages of completion, to ensure adherence to quality standards and approved timelines. Reviewing the progress of works under the Irrigation & Flood Control Department, the Minister directed that de-silting of water channels and strengthening of flood-protection infrastructure and embankments along vulnerable stretches be undertaken and completed on priority. Rana asked the Chief Engineer, I&FC, to furnish a river-wise status report detailing the progress of flood-protection works and the preparedness of vulnerable areas ahead of the winter season. He stressed that physical progress and financial expenditure must move in tandem and that funds allocated for developmental works should be utilised judiciously, transparently and within the prescribed timelines.

stories.title: After damning reports on CEC, Tejashwi Yadav seeks re-election in Bihar and West Bengal
stories.summary: He also alleged that Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Union Home Minister Amit Shah are misusing constitutional institutions and treating them like wings of the Bharatiya Janata Party

article_sentences: Bihar Leader of Opposition Tejashwi Yadav on Wednesday (September 23, 2026) said a report regarding the Election Commission’s functioning has revealed how the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) intends to dismantle the Constitution and democracy, and how Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Union Home Minister Amit Shah are destroying the democratic system.

Addressing the media at his official residence in Patna, the Rashtriya Janata Dal (RJD) national working president asserted that serious questions have arisen from the report, and both Election Commissioners have lodged complaints regarding the Chief Election Commissioner’s modus operandi.
“Why is there silence over the questions raised by the two Election Commissioners about the Chief Election Commissioner of India (ECI) Gyanesh Kumar?
He should come forward and answer.
The press release issued by the ECI was drafted at the behest of Amit Shah,” Mr. Yadav alleged.
He pointed out that when the special intensive revision (SIR) was under way in Bihar, the RJD was the first to raise questions and even approached the Supreme Court seeking justice.
Mr. Yadav further alleged that the report has revealed that the Chief Election Commissioner enjoys the BJP’s patronage.

“It has also become clear how the ‘SIR’ process was arbitrarily implemented across the country, including in Bihar and West Bengal and how the Commission abused its authority to help the BJP to win elections in these States and other States.
Despite lodging a complaint against Gyanesh Kumar’s arbitrary actions and working style, the Commission cunningly altered the rules to eliminate evidence.
It has also come to light how the Commission blatantly flouted the rules,” Mr. Yadav alleged.

The RJD leader further said that previously, the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court played a role in the selection of the Chief Election Commissioner, but the Narendra Modi government changed this process to include a Union Minister instead.
“Elections in Bihar were conducted fraudulently.

stories.headline: Opposition calls for CEC Gyanesh Kumar’s removal after report on Election Commissioners’ dissent
stories.title: Opposition calls for CEC Gyanesh Kumar’s removal after report on Election Commissioners’ dissent
stories.summary: Both ECs recorded formal objections regarding centralisation of poll roll database, “illegal” changes in Form 6, removal of voters in West Bengal, Goa; terming the CEC the “chief architect of vote chori”, Congress calls for SC-monitored probe
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Opposition parties on Wednesday (September 23, 2026) sought the removal of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar after an Indian Express expose claimed that two of the three Election Commissioners, Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, had formally recorded objections at least 14 times over the last 10 months.
The two ECs said major decisions were being made in the name of the full Election Commission of India without their knowledge, several of which they called “unauthorised and illegal”.

Declaring that “vote chori” is a crime against the Indian people and a direct attack on the Constitution, the Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi said that “the BJP, RSS and EC who organised it have committed an act of treason.
Justice will be served.” He will hold a press conference on the matter on Thursday.

Opposition parties asked the Supreme Court to take suo motu cognisance of the report and Congress leader K.C. Venugopal demanded a Supreme Court-monitored impartial investigation to “expose the rot that has destroyed the ECI’s credibility”.
The CEC has no right to remain in office after the expose, he said.
The ECI responded on Wednesday (September 23, 2026), saying that all its actions have been in accordance with laws and instructions of the Commission.

Highlighting specific internal notes or observations spread over the 10-month period while overlooking the much larger body of approvals, decisions, instructions, and initiatives gives only “one part of the picture”, it said.
According to the Indian Express report, both Election Commissioners red-flagged several key issues, led by the centralisation of the database of electoral rolls.
In May, Mr. Joshi had reportedly proposed an audit to certify that “no one except the concerned statutory authorities has any credentials to make any change in the data base”.

In August, Mr. Sandhu had recorded that State-level election officials were reporting that they do not have “proper and complete access” to the ERONet portal, the digital system through which the electoral rolls are maintained.

He further flagged that the Commission’s director general of information technology Seema Khanna “does not have any legal authority to restrict proper and complete access and freedom to operate as given by law to the statutory authorities”.

stories.headline: Private hospitals oppose NAPS push
stories.title: Private hospitals oppose NAPS push
stories.summary: Srinagar, Sep 23: The J&K Hospitals and Dialysis Centres Association (JKPHDA) on Wednesday expressed serious concern over the manner in which the National Apprenticeship Promotion Scheme (NAPS) under Skill India is being pushed in the private health sector in J&K. The NAPS, launched by the Prime Minister under Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship in 2015, is a 6 to 12 months training program where 75 percent of stipend is borne by the establishment and 25 percent by the Govt. of India. The JKPHDA stated that the majority of private hospitals are already registered under NAPS and as and when vacancies arise, the same are uploaded on the portal as per norms. However, what is happening for the last few weeks is a matter of concern for the owners of the private hospitals across the UT. The association said Chief Medical Officers are summoning owners of hospitals, nursing homes, clinical establishments to their offices and directing them to create vacancies on war footing and take apprentices under NAPS. It said the members feel this coercive approach is not in the spirit of a voluntary skill program. “All private hospitals empanelled under Ayushman Bharat, SEHAT scheme haven’t received payments for last 8-10 months from State Health Agency (SHA) and liabilities have crossed crores.” “To sustain, hospitals have curtailed services and even terminated some employees. In this situation, how can we bear the 75 percent stipend burden of new apprentices.” “The association said hospitals have their own HR policy- face-to-face interview, skill test and verification. Under the present mechanism being forced, there is no interaction with candidates before posting, which is a serious risk in the patient care sector,” it stated. The Association said it is optional for establishments having a workforce between 4-29 and establishments having a workforce of 3 or less are not permitted to engage apprentices but unfortunately are being forced for the same. “As per our information, about 40,000 regular posts are lying vacant with the Govt. Instead of advertising those regular posts, this ad-hoc arrangement is being pushed to show inflated employment figures,” it stated. The JKPHDA also expressed surprise over the sudden haste and coercive manner in which targets are being pushed at ground level in the last few weeks, which is contrary to the voluntary spirit of the scheme since 2015. “The private health sector is not against Skill India. We have always supported skilling and employment. But you can’t force employment generation on a sector which is itself struggling for survival due to non-payment of dues for 8-10 months,” the association added. The association requested Lieutenant Governor Manoj Sinha and the Chief Minister to release pending SEHAT payments of private hospitals. They seek to make NAPS implementation voluntary and need-based in the health sector as originally envisaged in 2015, not forced. “Advertise the 40,000 vacant regular posts with Govt so that youth get permanent employment, not 6-month stipend.” The association hoped that the government will look into the genuine difficulties of the health sector, which is providing 70 percent of healthcare under SEHAT scheme in J&K.

stories.headline: The Rupee, the Oil Barrel and the Common Indian
stories.title: The Rupee, the Oil Barrel and the Common Indian
stories.summary: The common Indian does not wake up in the morning thinking about the rupee-dollar exchange rate or the international price of crude oil. He is more likely to think about the price of vegetables, the cost of filling his scooter, the school fees due at the end of the month or whether there will be enough left in the bank account after the electricity bill is paid. Yet, strangely enough, a part of the answer to each of these everyday concerns may be connected to events taking place thousands of kilometres away, in markets where oil is traded in dollars and currencies move in response to forces that an ordinary household can neither see nor influence. That is the curious nature of the modern economy. Something can happen in a distant oil field, a financial market or a geopolitical flashpoint and, after passing through several invisible channels, arrive quietly at the doorstep of an Indian family. The distance between an oil barrel in an international market and a cooking stove in an Indian kitchen may appear enormous, but economically the two are not as far apart as they seem. The recent pressure on the rupee and the rise in international crude prices have brought that connection into sharper focus. The rupee has been trading around the mid-90s against the US dollar, while crude prices have moved above the $100-a-barrel mark amid geopolitical uncertainty and concerns about supplies. The Reserve Bank of India has intervened to contain excessive volatility, but a country as dependent on imported crude as India cannot remain completely insulated from developments in the global oil market. For the financial world, these movements are expressed through charts, percentages and exchange rates. For an ordinary household, their meaning is much simpler: how much does it cost to travel, to transport goods, to cook, to run a business and, ultimately, to live? Oil has a peculiar place in the economy because its influence extends far beyond the fuel station. A truck carrying vegetables from a farm to a city market needs fuel. So does the vehicle carrying milk, medicines or manufactured goods. Farmers depend on fuel for machinery and irrigation in many parts of the country. Businesses pay for transportation, and transportation costs eventually become part of the price of what they sell. The effect is therefore not confined to motorists. Even someone who rarely travels by car can encounter the consequences of expensive oil through the prices of goods and services. This is where an international economic story becomes a domestic one. A rise in crude prices does not necessarily mean that every price in India will rise immediately. There are several factors between international oil prices and the final price paid by a consumer. Companies may absorb some of the additional cost, governments may alter taxes or other policies, currency movements may strengthen or weaken the impact, and changing supply conditions can provide relief. But if elevated costs persist, pressure can gradually spread through the economy. The household usually notices the result long before it understands the process. It notices that the monthly budget has become tighter. It notices that a journey which once cost a certain amount now requires more money. It notices that the vegetable seller has increased prices or that the delivery charge has changed. A small business owner notices that transporting goods has become more expensive. A parent notices the rising cost of getting children to school or tuition. None of them may know what Brent crude is trading at, but all of them understand what an additional burden means. That is the real story behind inflation. It is not merely a number announced in an economic report. It is the difference between what a family earned yesterday and what that income can purchase today. The rupee adds another layer to this story. Since crude oil is traded internationally in dollars, a weaker rupee can make imported oil more expensive in domestic currency even if the international price of oil remains unchanged. When the price of oil rises at the same time that the rupee weakens, the pressure can become more pronounced. The effect does not move in a straight line, but the underlying vulnerability remains. India cannot control the price at which crude is sold in international markets. It cannot determine the value of the dollar or dictate the course of geopolitical events that disrupt global energy supplies. Yet the Indian consumer ultimately has to live with the economic consequences of these forces. There is something unsettling about that imbalance. The decisions that affect a household budget may be made in places the household will never see and by forces over which it has no control. A war in one part of the world can influence fuel prices in another. A change in American interest rates can affect capital flows and the value of emerging-market currencies. A disruption in an international shipping route can increase transportation costs. A rise in crude prices can alter inflationary pressures across countries. The modern economy has erased many of the boundaries that once separated distant events from local life. The world has become economically smaller, but the consequences of that interconnectedness are not always evenly distributed. A family with considerable financial room may absorb a rise in everyday expenses without making major changes. For a household already managing its finances carefully, the same increase can mean postponing a purchase, reducing travel, cutting discretionary spending or drawing upon savings. The headline inflation rate may look modest, but its effect depends greatly on where a family begins. This is why purchasing power matters as much as income. A salary increase may look satisfactory on paper, but if essential expenses rise at the same time, the feeling of improvement may not reach the household. What matters to a family is not simply how many rupees it earns but what those rupees can actually buy. The pressure can also travel through interest rates. If persistent oil-driven inflation becomes a concern, monetary policy may have to respond. Higher interest rates can make borrowing more expensive, affecting home loans, business credit and other forms of borrowing. An external oil shock can therefore reach the citizen through several channels, sometimes without the citizen ever knowing where the chain began. This is why energy security is ultimately a human issue, not merely a strategic one. India's growing investment in renewable energy, electric mobility, energy efficiency and other alternatives is therefore significant beyond the language of climate policy. Reducing dependence on imported fossil fuels can also reduce exposure to sudden international price shocks. Every additional source of domestic energy and every improvement in efficiency can, over time, provide a degree of protection to the economy and to consumers. But resilience is not created only through national policy. It also has a household dimension. A family with savings, manageable debt and some financial flexibility is better placed to absorb an unexpected increase in expenses than one whose entire income is already committed. Unfortunately, such flexibility is difficult to build for millions of households when essential expenditure consumes most of the monthly income. That is why a seemingly small increase in the price of fuel or food can have consequences far beyond the amount printed on a receipt. The same is true for small businesses. A large corporation may be able to negotiate contracts, adjust supply chains or absorb temporary increases in operating costs. A small trader, transport operator, manufacturer or service provider may have far less room to manoeuvre. When costs rise, the choices can become uncomfortable: increase prices and risk losing customers, absorb the increase and reduce margins, or cut expenditure elsewhere. The common Indian economy is therefore not an abstraction. It is made up of millions of such decisions. There is also a psychological dimension to rising costs that economic statistics do not always capture. People begin to become cautious. They postpone purchases. They think twice before travelling. They become reluctant to take on new loans. They worry about education, healthcare and retirement. Even when the economy continues to grow, uncertainty can influence how confidently people spend and invest. For this reason, the health of an economy cannot be understood only through its large numbers. Growth matters. Investment matters. Foreign-exchange reserves matter. Fiscal stability matters. But so does the ability of an ordinary family to live without constantly feeling that one unexpected increase in expenditure can disturb the entire month's calculation. The rupee, in this sense, has two lives. In financial markets it is a currency whose value is measured against other currencies. In the lives of ordinary people, it is a measure of purchasing power. A rupee saved today represents a certain amount of food, transport, medicine, education or other necessities. When its purchasing power weakens, the change is felt not in the abstract but in what that money can no longer comfortably provide. This is why the discussion about the rupee should not be reduced to whether it has gained or lost a few paise against the dollar. Currency movements are influenced by a complicated combination of oil prices, global interest rates, capital flows, trade conditions, investor sentiment and domestic economic factors. There is rarely a single explanation. But behind the complexity lies a simple concern: how resilient is the economy when external pressures accumulate? India has important strengths. Its large domestic market, diversified economy, foreign-exchange reserves and policy institutions provide buffers against external shocks. The Reserve Bank has tools to manage excessive volatility, and the country's growing energy diversification offers another layer of protection. But resilience does not mean immunity. No major oil-importing economy can completely escape the consequences of a prolonged surge in global crude prices. The larger lesson is therefore not about predicting where the rupee will trade tomorrow or where crude oil will settle next week. Markets will continue to move, sometimes for reasons that become clear only afterwards. The more important question is whether India's economic foundations are strong enough to ensure that external shocks do not become an unbearable burden for ordinary citizens. Because the final destination of an economic shock is rarely a financial market. It is a household. It is the person calculating whether the month's salary will cover the month's expenses. It is the parent deciding whether an additional journey can be afforded. It is the small shopkeeper wondering whether customers will accept a higher price. It is the young couple managing a home loan while trying to save for their children's future. It is the elderly person watching the cost of essential goods rise while depending on a fixed income. This is why the oil barrel matters even to those who have never seen one, and why the rupee matters even to those who have never traded a dollar. The global economy may operate through enormous markets, sophisticated financial instruments and complicated chains of supply, but its consequences eventually become intensely personal. A movement on a distant screen can become an extra amount paid at a fuel station, a higher transport bill, a more expensive household purchase or a little less money left at the end of the month. Perhaps that is the most important way to understand the relationship between the rupee, oil and the common Indian. The oil barrel may be priced in a distant market, and the rupee may move in response to forces beyond our control, but the final arithmetic is often done at the kitchen table. And at that table, economics ceases to be a subject of charts and percentages. It becomes a question of whether a family's income can still stretch far enough to meet the life it has planned. opening: The common Indian does not wake up in the morning thinking about the rupee-dollar exchange rate or the international price of crude oil.

He is more likely to think about the price of vegetables, the cost of filling his scooter, the school fees due at the end of the month or whether there will be enough left in the bank account after the electricity bill is paid.
body: Yet, strangely enough, a part of the answer to each of these everyday concerns may be connected to events taking place thousands of kilometres away, in markets where oil is traded in dollars and currencies move in response to forces that an ordinary household can neither see nor influence.
That is the curious nature of the modern economy.
Something can happen in a distant oil field, a financial market or a geopolitical flashpoint and, after passing through several invisible channels, arrive quietly at the doorstep of an Indian family.
The distance between an oil barrel in an international market and a cooking stove in an Indian kitchen may appear enormous, but economically the two are not as far apart as they seem.
The recent pressure on the rupee and the rise in international crude prices have brought that connection into sharper focus.
The rupee has been trading around the mid-90s against the US dollar, while crude prices have moved above the $100-a-barrel mark amid geopolitical uncertainty and concerns about supplies.

The Reserve Bank of India has intervened to contain excessive volatility, but a country as dependent on imported crude as India cannot remain completely insulated from developments in the global oil market.
For the financial world, these movements are expressed through charts, percentages and exchange rates.
For an ordinary household, their meaning is much simpler: how much does it cost to travel, to transport goods, to cook, to run a business and, ultimately, to live?
Oil has a peculiar place in the economy because its influence extends far beyond the fuel station.
A truck carrying vegetables from a farm to a city market needs fuel.
So does the vehicle carrying milk, medicines or manufactured goods.
Farmers depend on fuel for machinery and irrigation in many parts of the country.
Businesses pay for transportation, and transportation costs eventually become part of the price of what they sell.
The effect is therefore not confined to motorists.
Even someone who rarely travels by car can encounter the consequences of expensive oil through the prices of goods and services.
This is where an international economic story becomes a domestic one.
A rise in crude prices does not necessarily mean that every price in India will rise immediately.
There are several factors between international oil prices and the final price paid by a consumer.

Companies may absorb some of the additional cost, governments may alter taxes or other policies, currency movements may strengthen or weaken the impact, and changing supply conditions can provide relief.
But if elevated costs persist, pressure can gradually spread through the economy.
The household usually notices the result long before it understands the process.
It notices that the monthly budget has become tighter.
It notices that a journey which once cost a certain amount now requires more money.
It notices that the vegetable seller has increased prices or that the delivery charge has changed.
A small business owner notices that transporting goods has become more expensive.
A parent notices the rising cost of getting children to school or tuition.
None of them may know what Brent crude is trading at, but all of them understand what an additional burden means.
That is the real story behind inflation.
It is not merely a number announced in an economic report.
It is the difference between what a family earned yesterday and what that income can purchase today.
The rupee adds another layer to this story.
Since crude oil is traded internationally in dollars, a weaker rupee can make imported oil more expensive in domestic currency even if the international price of oil remains unchanged.
When the price of oil rises at the same time that the rupee weakens, the pressure can become more pronounced.
The effect does not move in a straight line, but the underlying vulnerability remains.
India cannot control the price at which crude is sold in international markets.
It cannot determine the value of the dollar or dictate the course of geopolitical events that disrupt global energy supplies.
Yet the Indian consumer ultimately has to live with the economic consequences of these forces.
There is something unsettling about that imbalance.
The decisions that affect a household budget may be made in places the household will never see and by forces over which it has no control.
A war in one part of the world can influence fuel prices in another.
A change in American interest rates can affect capital flows and the value of emerging-market currencies.
A disruption in an international shipping route can increase transportation costs.
A rise in crude prices can alter inflationary pressures across countries.

The world has become economically smaller, but the consequences of that interconnectedness are not always evenly distributed.
A family with considerable financial room may absorb a rise in everyday expenses without making major changes.
For a household already managing its finances carefully, the same increase can mean postponing a purchase, reducing travel, cutting discretionary spending or drawing upon savings.
The headline inflation rate may look modest, but its effect depends greatly on where a family begins.

A salary increase may look satisfactory on paper, but if essential expenses rise at the same time, the feeling of improvement may not reach the household.
What matters to a family is not simply how many rupees it earns but what those rupees can actually buy.
The pressure can also travel through interest rates.
If persistent oil-driven inflation becomes a concern, monetary policy may have to respond.
Higher interest rates can make borrowing more expensive, affecting home loans, business credit and other forms of borrowing.
An external oil shock can therefore reach the citizen through several channels, sometimes without the citizen ever knowing where the chain began.
This is why energy security is ultimately a human issue, not merely a strategic one.
India's growing investment in renewable energy, electric mobility, energy efficiency and other alternatives is therefore significant beyond the language of climate policy.
Reducing dependence on imported fossil fuels can also reduce exposure to sudden international price shocks.
Every additional source of domestic energy and every improvement in efficiency can, over time, provide a degree of protection to the economy and to consumers.

stories.title: Supreme Court Reserves Order On Noida DM Medha Roopam's Plea To Stay Allahabad HC Judgment Quashing Student's NSA Detention

article_sentences: The Supreme Court today(September 23) reserved order on the grant of interim relief in the petition filed by Gautam Buddh Nagar District(Noida) Magistrate Medha Roopam challenging the Allahabad High Court order, which directed compensation of Rs.5 lakhs to be paid from her salary for the detention of student Akriti Chaudhary under the National Security Act in connection with the Noida workers' protest.
The Court also heard a separate petition filed by the State of Uttar Pradesh challenging the High Court's order quashing the NSA detention of the student.
A bench comprising Justice Satish Chandra Sharma and Justice NK Singh after hearing the matter, reserved it for interim orders.
The bench had muted the audio of the VC proceedings during the hearing, blocking media access (reporters cannot physically enter the Supreme Court).
It is understood that the State and the officer argued against isolating the DM for fixing liability over the student's detention.
They pressed for staying the High Court's order and its strictures against the bureaucrat.
Solicitor General of India Tushar Mehta, appearing for the District Magistrate, submitted that the strictures against the officer were "unwarranted".
He stated that there are several layers before the District Magistrate takes the decision.

Senior Advocate Mukul Rohatgi, for the State of UP, submitted that the Allahabad High Court's order is "totally uncalled for." He added that the respondent, Akriti Chaudhary, was "fomenting trouble" in Manesar in Haryana, and later the agitation shifted to Noida, which led to arson and destruction of public properties in April.
The proposal for detention was moved by the SHO, and ultimately passed by the DM.

The DM's order was approved by the advisory committee, and subsequently by the State Government and the Union Government under the National Security Act, he added, emphasising that the DM was only a "link in the chain." Rohatgi further contended that the High Court did not examine the NSA detention order, and its examination was only confined to whether the arrest was legal or not.
The audio of the proceedings was blocked at this juncture, denying further access to the proceedings.

stories.title: Cabinet approves ‘DURGA’ scheme for e-autos in Delhi
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence

candidate gate: no category but HIGH+ priority -> allowed
article_sentences: The Delhi Cabinet on Wednesday approved the ‘DURGA’ scheme to allocate electric autos exclusively to women and transgender persons, according to a statement from the Chief Minister’s Office.
In the first phase, 1,300 pink electric autos are proposed to be registered.
Of these, 1,170 will be allocated to women and 130 to transgender beneficiaries.
A maximum of 90 electric autos for women and 10 for transgender beneficiaries will be allocated in each revenue district.

The CMO stated the scheme aims to provide “dignified self-employment and livelihood opportunities” while promoting women’s safety, greater participation of transgender persons in the transport sector, last-mile connectivity and clean and sustainable urban transport.
The scheme, approved at a Cabinet meeting chaired by Chief Minister Rekha Gupta, is formally called the Upliftment and Rozgar for Women/Transgender Green E-Auto (DURGA) scheme.
Applicants will be able to apply through a dedicated online portal.
The benefits will be available to those who meet the prescribed eligibility criteria.
According to the eligibility criteria, applicants must be Delhi residents aged 20 to 40 and have a valid voter identity card, an LMW driving licence and a PSV (Public Service Vehicle) badge.
A woman with more than three children will not be eligible.
The applicant’s family must also not own any registered transport vehicle or three-wheeler.
The applicant’s family income must not exceed ₹5 lakh.

stories.title: Supreme Court stays High Court order to recover ₹5 lakh from Noida DM in NSA detention case
stories.summary: Appearing for Medha Roopam, senior advocate Mukul Rohatgi submitted that such decisions went through a multi-tiered process and his client cannot be singled out for penalty
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: The Supreme Court on Wednesday (September 23, 2026) stayed an Allahabad High Court direction to recover ₹5 lakh from the salary of Gautam Buddha Nagar District Magistrate Medha Roopam and other officials to compensate Delhi University student Akriti Chaudhary for detaining her under the National Security Act (NSA) over a workers’ protest in Noida in April this year.
A Bench headed by Justice Satish Chandra Sharma froze the operation of the Division Bench judgment, which quashed the student’s nearly five-month detention as illegal.

Appearing for Ms. Roopam, senior advocate Mukul Rohatgi submitted that such decisions went through a multi-tiered process, including at the Central and State levels, and his client cannot be singled out for penalty.
Senior Advocate Tushar Mehta, who is the Solicitor General of India, also appeared on the side of Ms. Roopam.
Senior Advocate Colin Gonsalves appeared for Ms. Chaudhary, the respondent in the case.
“After hearing senior counsels for the parties, this court is of the opinion that till the matter is heard on merits, the operation of the judgment, particularly paragraphs nos.
27 to 33, shall remain stayed,” the court ordered, listing the case for October 7.

The seven paragraphs highlighted by the Supreme Court from the High Court decision against Ms. Roopam had cautioned that the continued “despotic” conduct of an errant bureaucracy could reduce Uttar Pradesh to an “Orwellian Dystopia”.
The High Court had criticised Ms. Roopam’s lack of application of mind to a police report against the student activist.
It had allowed Ms. Chaudhary’s habeas corpus petition and ordered her immediate release, unless she was required in another case.
The High Court had flagged discrepancies in the arrest notice and termed the State’s version a “concocted story”.

Ms. Chaudhary was among several activists arrested in connection with the protest held between April 10 and 18, during which industrial and contractual workers demanded a hike and parity with wages paid in neighbouring Haryana.

stories.headline: Supreme Court Frowns Upon PIL Challenging Inter-Se Assessment Of Tender Bids
stories.title: Supreme Court Frowns Upon PIL Challenging Inter-Se Assessment Of Tender Bids
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: The Supreme Court on Wednesday (September 23) has observed that a ₹23-crore road construction contract was not of such magnitude as to justify a Public Interest Litigation (PIL) on the ground of alleged wastage of public resources, particularly when the dispute essentially concerned the comparative eligibility of competing bidders.

A Bench of Justice Dipankar Datta and Justice Sheel Nagu made the observation while hearing an appeal against a Himachal Pradesh High Court judgment that had quashed the award of a ₹23-crore Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana (“PMGSY”) road project in favour of the Appellant-O.P. Mehta and directed re-tendering.
The Court questioned whether such a tender dispute could appropriately be brought through a PIL, noting that the challenge predominantly involved an inter-se comparison between two bidders.

“We have our reservations since the grounds raised in the PIL before the High Court of Himachal Pradesh, Shimla pre-dominantly dealt with, inter-se comparative assessment between the two bidders whose bids had been received…”, the Court said.
Importantly, the Court noted that the value of the work, approximately ₹23 crore, was not by itself sufficient to invoke public interest on the ground of wastage of public resources.
“Moreso even the cost of work (Rs.
23 crores) was not of such magnitude, which may allow the petitioner in PIL to raise the plea of wastage of public resources.”, the Court observed.
The Court also noted that the PIL petitioner was the “alter ego of the unsuccessful bidder”, who had complained against the successful bidder and subsequently withdrawn the complaint.

Taking note of the appellant's assurance to complete the remaining work within three months at the original rates and without compromising quality, the Court granted the appellant three months to complete the project.
If the work is not completed within that period, the authorities have been directed to re-tender the work at the prevailing market rate.
The matter will be listed in the first week of December 2026 for a compliance report.
For Petitioner(s):Mr. Anup Rattan, Advocate General Mr. Vaibhav Srivastava, A.A.G. Mr. Puneet Rajta, Adv.

stories.title: EC must not only be independent but also be seen to act freely: SC judge
stories.summary: New Delhi: An umpire selected by the captain of a cricket team that eventually wins would always be suspected over his decisions even if they are correct, Supreme Court judge Dipankar Datta said on Wednesday to highlight that the Executive will have an “effective” veto in the selection of the Chief Election Commissioner and election […]

event term: 'supreme court' in summary weight 26.4
article_sentences: New Delhi: An umpire selected by the captain of a cricket team that eventually wins would always be suspected over his decisions even if they are correct, Supreme Court judge Dipankar Datta said on Wednesday to highlight that the Executive will have an “effective” veto in the selection of the Chief Election Commissioner and election commissioners.

Using this cricket metaphor, Justice Datta was extremely critical of the fact that a three-member panel, comprising the Prime Minister, the Leader of Opposition and a Union minister, selects the CEC and election commissioners.
If free and fair elections are to be ensured, it is axiomatic that the Election Commission (EC) must not only be an independent body but also be seen to act independently, he said.

Justice Datta headed a bench, also comprising Justice Satish Chandra Sharma, which gave split opinions on whether a batch of pleas challenging the validity of a 2023 law that excludes the CJI from the panel for selecting the chief election commissioner (CEC) and election commissioners should be referred to a larger constitution bench.

Dealing with the issue of independence and neutrality, Justice Datta noted the submissions of petitioners that the inclusion of a minister in the panel denuded the selection committee of institutional neutrality.
“If the said Selection Committee were to function, the decision would invariably be 2:1, on paper, in favour of the executive and, in practice, of whoever is the ruling party.
With two members from the executive being part of the Selection Committee, the executive has an effective veto,” he said.

Referring to discussion during the hearing, he said it was quite unlikely that the minister would take a stand against the Prime Minister in case of a difference of opinion between the Prime Minister and the Leader of Opposition.
“The presence of likelihood of a ‘no’ is striking enough to colour the perception of the Selection Committee; the probabilities and certainties of the ‘no’ matter little.
Thus, the challengers of the law contend, even if the appointments are meritorious, the process does not pass the perception test.

“The bottom line of the argument runs thus: it would not be a fallacious metaphor if it is said that since the umpire is picked by the captain of one side in a cricket match and his team wins, even if the decisions taken by such umpire are correct, it has the patina of suspicion, for, at the end of the day, the umpire has effectively been chosen by the winning captain,” he said.
Justice Sharma differed with the views of Justice Datta and batted for referring the pleas to a larger bench while terming the issue as important.
